title: Straight from the CEO: The World's Top Business Leaders Reveal Ideas That Every Manager Can Use
author: Edited by G. William Dauphinais and Colin Price
summary:
*Straight from the CEO* is a 1998 compilation edited by G. William Dauphinais and Colin Price, both then affiliated with the consulting firm Price Waterhouse (later PricewaterhouseCoopers), gathering firsthand perspectives from roughly three dozen chief executives of major global corporations. Rather than a single authorial voice offering a unified theory of leadership, the book is structured around a series of pressing management issues — customer loyalty, global organization, employee motivation, corporate values, revitalization of struggling companies — with individual chapters or contributed pieces built around the reflections of specific CEOs, including leaders like Cor Herkströter of Royal Dutch/Shell, alongside executives from companies such as British Airways, OshKosh B'Gosh, Pitney Bowes, and Swisscom.

The editors' framing device is that most management books offer theory or consultant frameworks at some remove from the actual experience of running a company, while this book instead lets top executives describe, largely in their own words or paraphrased close to it, how they've actually approached major strategic and organizational challenges. Analytical sidebars from Dauphinais and Price accompany the executive contributions, adding context, comparison across the featured companies, and connecting individual CEO perspectives back to broader management themes the editors identify as recurring across the collection.

Reader and reviewer reaction to the book has been mixed on a specific structural point: because the individual executive contributions are, by design, brief, several readers and reviewers have noted that the pieces can feel more like short reflections or interview excerpts than fully developed chapters, occasionally leaving readers wanting more depth on any single perspective even as the breadth of contributors is the book's clear selling point. The book functioned as a kind of snapshot of late-1990s global executive thinking on then-pressing issues like globalization, and the same editorial team (with an additional co-author, Grady Means) later produced a follow-up compilation, *Wisdom of the CEO*, extending the same format to a fresh set of executives and challenges.

Because this is fundamentally a multi-author compilation of first-person executive reflections curated and framed by two editors, rather than a single sustained authorial argument, the "sections" and "key lessons" below are organized around the book's major thematic clusters as documented in available secondary sources, rather than a claim to reproduce or closely paraphrase any individual CEO's specific contributed content, which this project's copyright rules require treating with particular care given the compilation format and this entry's limited direct access to the original text.

sections.title: Customer Loyalty and Service
sections.summary:
This thematic section gathers CEO perspectives on how their organizations approached building and sustaining customer loyalty, a recurring priority across the featured companies regardless of industry. The editors frame customer loyalty as a strategic asset that top executives increasingly treated as core to competitive positioning rather than a secondary operational concern delegated entirely to service departments.

Based on available secondary descriptions, the contributed material in this cluster draws on executives describing specific organizational choices — investment in service culture, structural changes to put executives closer to customer experience, and using customer feedback more directly in strategic decision-making — that they credited with improving loyalty outcomes at their companies.

This section transitions into the collection's next major theme: how these same organizations approached the challenge of operating and coordinating across increasingly global operations.
keyLessons: Several featured CEOs treated customer loyalty as a core strategic asset, not a delegated operational afterthought.
Structural choices that put leadership closer to actual customer experience were a recurring theme across contributors.
Direct use of customer feedback in strategic decision-making was credited by multiple executives with improved loyalty outcomes.

sections.title: Organizing Globally
sections.summary:
This section compiles executive reflections on the organizational challenges of operating across many countries and cultures — a pressing topic in the late 1990s as globalization accelerated for many of the featured companies, including Royal Dutch/Shell under Cor Herkströter's leadership.

The contributed material addresses tensions between global standardization (consistency, efficiency, brand coherence) and local responsiveness (adapting to different markets, regulatory environments, and cultural expectations), with different executives describing different balances struck for their specific industries and company histories.

This section transitions into the collection's material on employee motivation, since several contributors connected effective global organization to how well a company could motivate and retain talent across very different local contexts.
keyLessons: Executives grappled with the tension between global standardization and local market responsiveness, with different companies striking different balances.
Organizing globally required different structural approaches depending on industry, regulatory environment, and company history.
Effective global organization was linked by several contributors to a company's ability to motivate and retain talent across diverse local contexts.

sections.title: Individual Employee Motivation
sections.summary:
This section gathers CEO reflections specifically on motivating individual employees across large, often geographically dispersed organizations, a theme the editors highlight as a top managerial priority among the executives featured.

Based on available secondary descriptions, contributed material in this cluster covers approaches to communication, recognition, and creating a sense of ownership or stake in company outcomes as tools for sustaining motivation at scale, drawn from the specific experience of each contributing executive's organization.

This section transitions into the book's material on corporate values, since several contributors connected sustained employee motivation to a genuinely lived, rather than merely stated, set of organizational values.
keyLessons: Communication and recognition practices were recurring themes in how featured executives described sustaining motivation at scale.
Several contributors linked a sense of ownership or stake in outcomes to stronger individual motivation.
Motivation strategies were described as varying meaningfully with company size, geography, and industry context.

sections.title: Leveraging Corporate Values to Enhance Performance
sections.summary:
This section compiles reflections on how corporate values — genuinely embedded rather than merely stated in a mission document — were used by the featured executives as a performance lever, connecting values explicitly to strategic and operational decision-making rather than treating them as a separate communications exercise.

The contributed material addresses how some executives worked to make values operational: embedding them into decision criteria, performance evaluation, and organizational storytelling, with the editors' sidebars drawing comparisons across how different companies approached this challenge.

This section transitions into the collection's closing material on revitalization, since several contributors connected a return to core values with successfully turning around underperforming parts of their organizations.
keyLessons: Several featured executives worked to make corporate values operational — embedded in decisions and evaluation, not just stated in mission documents.
Genuine, lived values were presented as a performance lever, not solely a communications or branding exercise.
Approaches to embedding values varied across companies and were shaped by each organization's specific culture and history.

sections.title: Revitalization
sections.summary:
The book's closing thematic section addresses how featured executives approached revitalizing underperforming companies or business units, a recurring challenge among the roughly three dozen leaders included in the collection.

Based on available secondary descriptions, contributed material in this cluster covers specific turnaround strategies described by different executives, connecting back to themes from earlier sections — customer focus, global organization, employee motivation, and corporate values — as levers used in combination during periods of organizational renewal.

This section closes the collection by tying its major recurring themes together, with the editors' closing analysis drawing out the patterns they observed across the roughly three dozen executive perspectives gathered in the book.
keyLessons: Revitalization strategies described by featured executives typically combined several of the book's other major themes (customer focus, values, motivation) rather than relying on a single lever.
Turnaround approaches varied substantially by industry and company-specific circumstances among the executives featured.
The editors used the revitalization theme to draw together patterns observed across the full collection of executive perspectives.
Treat customer loyalty as a core strategic asset connected directly to leadership decisions, not solely a delegated operational function.
Balance global standardization with local market responsiveness deliberately, rather than defaulting entirely to one approach.
Use communication, recognition, and genuine ownership-sharing to sustain employee motivation across large or dispersed organizations.
Make corporate values operational — embedded in decisions and evaluation — rather than treating them as a separate communications exercise.
Approach organizational revitalization by combining multiple levers (customer focus, values, motivation, structure) rather than relying on one alone.
Recognize that management approaches that work in one industry or company culture may not transfer directly to another; context shapes which lever matters most.
Value the perspective of practitioners who have actually run large organizations alongside, not instead of, academic and consulting frameworks.

whoThisIsFor: Managers and business students interested in pattern-spotting across how different global CEOs of the late 1990s approached common strategic challenges, rather than readers looking for a single unified leadership framework.
whenToReadThis: Best read selectively, by theme (customer loyalty, globalization, motivation, values, or revitalization), rather than cover to cover, given its compilation format.

authorBio.name: G. William Dauphinais and Colin Price (editors)
authorBio.bio:
G. William Dauphinais worked in brand management, marketing, and communication at PricewaterhouseCoopers and had previously co-authored two earlier business books, *The Paradox Principles* and *Better Change*, before co-editing *Straight from the CEO*.

Colin Price built a long consulting career advising major corporations, national governments, and charitable institutions, later serving as Group Chief Operating Officer at Quintet Private Bank. Beyond *Straight from the CEO*, he has co-authored several other business books, including *Beyond Performance* (with Scott Keller), *Mergers* (with David Fubini and Maurizio Zollo), and *Vertical Take-Off* (with Sir Richard Evans). He holds degrees in economics, industrial relations and psychology, and organizational behavior, and has held academic affiliations including as an associate fellow of Saïd Business School at Oxford University and a visiting professor at Imperial College London.

Together, Dauphinais and Price worked at the management consulting firm Price Waterhouse (later PricewaterhouseCoopers) when they compiled this book, drawing on the firm's access to senior executive relationships across its global client base to assemble contributions from roughly three dozen CEOs.

conceptsFrameworks.name: (No named, author-coined frameworks confirmed)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: As a multi-author compilation of individual CEO reflections curated by two editors, *Straight from the CEO* is organized around thematic issues (customer loyalty, global organization, motivation, values, revitalization) rather than a single named model, framework, or law coined by the editors. No specific named framework could be verified for this entry, and none has been invented to fill this section, consistent with the project's honesty requirement.

actionSteps: Identify one place in your own organization or role where customer feedback could be brought more directly into strategic (not just operational) decision-making, and propose a specific change.
If you operate across multiple locations or contexts, map where you currently default to standardization versus local adaptation, and identify one place where that default may be wrong.
Audit whether your organization's stated values actually show up in how decisions and performance are evaluated, and identify one concrete gap to close.

Identify one underperforming area of your work or organization and sketch a revitalization plan that combines at least two levers (e.g., customer focus and employee motivation) rather than relying on a single fix.
Interview or informally survey a handful of colleagues about what genuinely motivates them at work, and compare it against what your organization currently emphasizes.
reflectionQuestions: Where does your organization talk about customer loyalty as a value versus actually structuring decisions around it?
If you operate in more than one market or team culture, where have you seen standardization backfire, or local adaptation go too far?
What would it look like for your organization's stated values to show up more concretely in how people are evaluated and promoted?
What combination of levers might a genuine revitalization effort in your own work actually require?

points: As a compilation of relatively brief executive contributions, several reader and reviewer sources describe individual pieces as feeling more like short reflections or interview excerpts than fully developed chapters, which can leave readers wanting more depth on any single executive's perspective.

The book reflects a specific historical moment (published 1998, with contributors drawn from major corporations of that era) and specific challenges like globalization strategy that were especially prominent then; some of the referenced companies and executives may no longer hold the market positions described in the original text.

Because the book was produced by consultants at Price Waterhouse featuring executives likely to have been client relationships or prospective clients, readers should weigh the possibility that contributor selection and framing may have been shaped by those professional relationships, even though the underlying executive perspectives themselves may still be genuine and valuable.

The thematic, multi-contributor structure means the book offers breadth of perspective rather than a single, rigorously argued thesis — useful for pattern-spotting across leaders but less useful as a step-by-step management framework.
criticalTake.contextNote: Published in 1998, the book captures a specific late-1990s moment in global executive thinking, particularly around globalization strategy; readers should treat company-specific details and named executives' roles as reflecting that era rather than the present day, and the same editorial team's 1999 follow-up, *Wisdom of the CEO*, extended the format with a fresh set of contributors and challenges.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis based on general knowledge of the book's compilation format plus web verification of its editors, publication details, contributor examples (including Cor Herkströter of Royal Dutch/Shell and companies including British Airways, OshKosh B'Gosh, Pitney Bowes, and Swisscom), and a documented reader critique regarding chapter brevity, cross-checked against publisher and retailer listings in July 2026. No verified, verbatim quotations from the book's individual CEO contributors could be located through available sources, so the Highlights & Quotes section has been left empty rather than populated with invented or unverifiable attributions to named executives — flagged explicitly per this project's honesty rule, and treated with extra care given the compilation format involves quoting real, named business leaders.
